entry.title: Quit the Gym, Do Farmer Walks (Cheat Code)

media:group.media:title: Quit the Gym, Do Farmer Walks (Cheat Code)
media:group.media:description:
GRIP THEORY 12, twelve weeks of grip training with no gym (the heavy bucket hold, the towel hang, and when to go heavier): https://thereptheory.gumroad.com/l/grip
Pick up something heavy in each hand, and walk. Joe Rogan says carrying kettlebells up his driveway changed everything. So is he right? Here's what carrying heavy things does to your body, why the walking matters more than the weight, and a three-stage plan you can start at home tonight, with water jugs, shopping bags and a backpack of books.
What's in the video: • The bottle test: pinch the cap of a full 2-litre bottle, arm straight down, hold it as long as you can. Your number tells you which stage you start at. • It's not the weight: carrying the same weight made the core work harder than just holding it still (front, sides and lower back, on both sides). • Grip: the muscles that close your fingers sit in your forearm. In a study of almost 140,000 people in 17 countries, grip strength predicted how long people lived better than blood pressure did (a link, not proof). • How to do it: bend your knees, flat back, stand tall, shoulders down, short quick steps, 30 seconds. • What one carry stands in for: shrugs, a hand gripper, and a hard session. • Can it build muscle? A little, and a lot of strength on the row. The gym still won on the squat and the pull from the floor: carries are best added to lifting. • The one-hand twist: the suitcase carry, and the bear-hug carry. • The body-weight target: your full body weight in total, half in each hand, for 30 seconds. At 60 kg that's 30 in each hand, at home. • The plan: three days a week, three stages (a third, two thirds, then your full body weight), plus carry lunges and push-ups. • Your bottle test result: under 30 s → stage 1, farmer + suitcase only for 2 weeks · 30–60 s → stage 1 · 60–90 s → stage 2 · over 90 s → stage 3.
Safety first: we're not licensed professionals, so train at your own risk. Hard is fine, painful isn't: if anything gives you sharp pain, put it down, and if it doesn't go away, see a licensed physician right away. This video is general information, not medical advice. Results depend on where you start. The stages, times, body-weight target and test tiers are our own rough guide, not a lab test.

entry.title: How Training Tendons Makes You Insane at Pull Ups

media:group.media:title: How Training Tendons Makes You Insane at Pull Ups
media:group.media:description:
TENDON THEORY, 12 weeks of holds written out (every hold, how long, how heavy, when to go up; the bar hang and a doorframe row hold for your elbows): https://thereptheory.gumroad.com/l/tendons
A bodybuilder twice his size can't do five pull-ups. The skinny guy next to him does twenty. The difference isn't muscle. In the research, pull-ups had almost nothing to do with maximum pulling strength and a lot to do with strength for your own body weight. And every pull-up hangs your whole body off a few cables: the tendons in your fingers, your elbows and your shoulders.
Three holds that train those cables, one slow rep that ties them together, and a plan to go from a few pull-ups to a lot. No equipment beyond a bar and a chair.
What's in the video: • The hang test: arms straight, shoulders pulled down, hang as long as you can. Your number tells you where to start. • Why tendons matter: twelve weeks of hard 20-second holds made tendons 57% stiffer. Quick reps built the same strength, but only the holds made the tendons stiffer. • Stiff vs loose: a loose tendon is a bungee cord, the bar moves late. A stiff one is a chain. • Why elbows get sore: muscles get stronger faster than tendons. The muscle is ready, the cable isn't. • Hold 1, the bar hang: 3 × 30 to 45 seconds at about 7 out of 10 effort. Longer than 45? Go heavier with a backpack, not longer. • Hold 2, the shoulder-blade hold: 5 × 5 seconds, the first inch of every pull-up. • Hold 3, the three-angle hold: top, halfway and near-straight arms, 5 seconds each, 3 rounds. • The slow rep: the 5-second negative, 5 reps. Can't do 5 seconds yet? Start with 3 and add one a week. • The plan: small clean sets (can do 6? do 4s), one rep more a week, stop with 1 or 2 reps left, three days a week, think twelve weeks, not two. • Your hang test result: under 30 s → the bar hang and the slow reps first · 30 to 60 s → the whole plan · 60 to 90 s → add the backpack · over 90 s → weighted top and halfway holds.
Tendons aren't the whole story: your weight and practice matter too. They're just the part almost nobody trains on purpose.
Comment your hang-test time, and retest in four weeks.
Safety first: we're not licensed professionals, so train at your own risk. Hard is fine, painful isn't: if anything gives you sharp pain, stop, and if it doesn't go away, see a licensed physician right away. This video is general information, not medical advice. Results depend on where you start. The holds, times, plan and test tiers are our own rough guide, not a lab test.

entry.title: I'll Prove You Can Do a Handstand (Even as a Beginner)

media:group.media:title: I'll Prove You Can Do a Handstand (Even as a Beginner)
media:group.media:description:
REP THEORY 90, the 90-day plan on sale right now: https://thereptheory.gumroad.com/l/rt90
If you can do five push-ups, you can do a handstand. I'll prove it. A handstand isn't held up by your shoulders, it's steered by your fingers: in the research, more than three quarters of the balancing came from the wrists. We follow Day 1 from his first second upside down to his first handstand, through six steps. Every step has a number to hit before you earn the next one.
A handstand for beginners progression at home with no equipment, from zero to your first 2-second freestanding hold. Built for skinny guys: the lighter you are, the less your fingers have to catch.
What's in the video: • The pike test: hands down, hips up, shoulders over your hands, and count the seconds. Your result at the end tells you which step you start on. • How a handstand really works: your palm carries your weight, your fingers steer. Gymnasts correct a wobble in about a fifth of a second, and the wrist flexors work harder than any other muscle. • Why skinny guys have the edge: the work your fingers do to catch the same wobble grows with your body weight. • Step 1, finger presses: 3 sets of 10. Shift your shoulders past your hands and press your fingertips into the floor. • Step 2, the straight line: the overhead reach check, then a 30-second hollow hold with your lower back flat. • Step 3, the chair pike: 30 seconds, arms locked, pushing tall. Your shoulders' real job. • Step 4, chest to the wall: 30 seconds, hands one hand-length from the wall. • Step 5, the bail: the cartwheel bail, 10 each side, from almost straight upside down. The step almost nobody practises. • Step 6, leave the wall: float your toes off by one centimetre, then 2 seconds with nothing touching but your hands. • Why most people fall in the first second: the wrong shape, looking at your feet, and late corrections. • From two seconds to ten: the soft kick-up. • How to train it: about 10 minutes most days, your current step plus the one before it, stop when the holds get shaky. • Your pike test result: under 10 s → step 1 · 10–29 s → step 2 · 30–59 s → step 3 · a minute or more → step 4.
Comment your pike-test number and the step you're starting on.
Safety first: we're not licensed professionals, so train at your own risk. Warm up your wrists every session. Being upside down raises the pressure in your eyes, so breathe, don't strain, and come down if you get dizzy. If anything causes pain, stop and see a licensed physician right away. This video is general information, not medical advice. The step numbers and the test tiers are our own rough guide, not a lab test.

entry.title: Boost Your Bone Density With This 3 Minute Habit (life changing)

media:group.media:title: Boost Your Bone Density With This 3 Minute Habit (life changing)
media:group.media:description:
REFORGE 60, the 60-day strength plan + the Coach on Telegram: https://shop.reptheory.online/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=bones
Built for your body type, home or gym, with a personal coach on Telegram that keeps track of your workouts and reminds you when you're due. The Coach is an AI, not a person. 18+. A strength plan, not a bone plan: everything for your bones is in this video. Results depend on where you start.
A three-minute habit can change your bones for life, and I'll prove it. Bone is alive: every time you load it hard, it adds new bone right where the force went. A tennis player's racket arm carries up to about a quarter more bone mineral than the other arm. Your bones only answer to three things: impact, short bursts and new angles.
How to increase bone density naturally, at home, with no equipment: the bone density exercises that work, how to make your bones stronger and thicker, and jumping for bone density done right. Built for skinny guys.
What's in the video: • The jump test: your result at the end tells you where to start • 3 rules (impact beats time, short bursts, new angles) and 4 moves: the drop jump, side hops, the fall push-up, the backpack split squat • How a bone knows you jumped: a network of about 42 billion living cells • The fittest men with the weakest bones, and won't this wreck your knees? • The skinny factor: muscle is the strongest link to how much bone a guy has • Teen lifters, the teen window, and why it's never too late • Astronauts, baseball players' throwing arms, and the bone you keep for life • The twist about "denser": bones grow thicker, not just packed tighter • Does milk build bone? And the plan: about 3 minutes a day

entry.title: I'll Prove You Can Do a Planche (Even as a Beginner)

media:group.media:title: I'll Prove You Can Do a Planche (Even as a Beginner)
media:group.media:description:
REP THEORY 90: the 90-day plan with the push-up base and the planche lean built in → https://thereptheory.gumroad.com/l/rt90
If you can hold a plank for 30 seconds, you can do a planche. I'll prove it. A planche isn't a strength trick, it's a lever: your hands are the pivot, your body is the bar, and the further your weight sits from your hands, the heavier you get. Shorten the bar, and your body can hold it. We follow Day 1 from his first face-plant to his first planche, through seven links. Every link has a number to hit before you earn the next one.
What's in the video: • The fingertip test: lean in a push-up position until your shoulders are over your fingertips and count the seconds. Your result at the end tells you which link you start on. • Why skinny guys have the edge: the load in a planche is your weight times its distance from your hands, and strength only rises with about the two-thirds power of body weight. Bigger people are stronger, but not as much stronger as they are heavier. That's why elite ring gymnasts average about 167 cm and 65 kg (and no, gymnastics doesn't make you short). • Link 1, the push-away plank: push the floor away and spread your shoulder blades. That's the serratus, the planche's secret muscle. Goal: 30 seconds. • Link 2, the planche lean: a knee push-up puts about half your weight on your hands, a push-up about two-thirds, a planche all of it. Lean one finger-width further each week. Goal: shoulders over your fingertips, 3 holds of 15 seconds. • Link 3, the frog stand: your feet leave the floor for the first time (put a pillow in front of your face). Goal: 30 seconds. • Link 4, the tendons: straight arms load the tendon at the front of your elbow and your wrists. Muscles adapt in weeks, tendons in months: in one study, strength was up about 30% after two months of holds, but the tendons only caught up in month three. About half of young gymnasts report wrist pain. Three rules: wrists first, one change a week, pain means stop. • Link 5, the lift-off: straight arms, round your back, lift your feet for a moment. Push-up handles, parallettes or two stacks of books work. Goal: 6 lift-offs of 2 seconds. Why the best planche drill is the planche itself. • Link 6, the tuck planche: knees tucked, arms locked, nothing touching but your hands. Goal: 10 seconds. That's your first planche. • The 3 ways people fake the tuck: bent elbows, not leaning far enough, and pinching the shoulder blades. • Link 7, the road to the full planche: advanced tuck, one leg out, straddle, full. The honest timeline: a tuck takes most people a few months, a full planche a year or two. • Train it like a skill: why four short sessions beat one brutal one, and why your tendons need the day in between. • The plan: 4 days a week, about 15 minutes. 2 minutes of wrists, 5 holds of your current link, 2 easy sets of the link before it, 3 sets of push-ups. Move up after two clean sessions in a row. • Your fingertip test result: under 5 s → link 1 · 5–14 s → link 2 · 15 s+ → link 3 · 30 s and easy → respect link 4.
Comment your fingertip-test number and your link, and reply the day you hold your first tuck planche.
Safety first: warm up your wrists every session, lean only as far as you can hold with straight arms, and stop on any sharp wrist or elbow pain. Under 18? Your tendons are still catching up with your muscles, so keep the holds short and stay on each link longer. This video is general information, not medical advice. The link numbers and the test tiers are our own rough guide, not a lab test.

entry.title: Why Training Tendons Is Basically Cheating at Arm Wrestling

media:group.media:title: Why Training Tendons Is Basically Cheating at Arm Wrestling
media:group.media:description:
TENDON THEORY: the 12-week plan that trains every tendon, not just your arm → https://gum.co/u/o8e5ailx
Want to beat bigger guys at arm wrestling? Train your tendons. In an arm wrestle, late loses. Your hand-closing muscles sit in your forearm, and their force reaches your fingers through tendons, so stiff tendons get it there first. This video covers the four moments every match comes down to (the go, the wrist, the squeeze and the line), the four home moves that train each one, a 20-minute plan, and the cup test to see where you start.
Safety first: keep your hand in front of your shoulder and in line with your elbow, never turn away from your arm, warm up first, and if you're beaten, let go. Under 18? Keep every hold at about 7/10, never all-out. This video is general information, not medical advice. The cup-test times are our own rough guide, not a lab test.
Free Telegram (we train together every day): https://t.me/thereptheory

entry.title: Calisthenics From Zero: The Full 90-Day Plan

media:group.media:title: Calisthenics From Zero: The Full 90-Day Plan
media:group.media:description:

Your 90-day Winter Arc, from zero, with nothing but your bodyweight and a few household items. This is a complete calisthenics roadmap for beginners: a home calisthenics workout plan with no gym and no equipment, built in three phases (the foundation, the build, the skills), plus the one day that decides whether you make it.
Phase 1 (days 1-30) builds the base every calisthenics routine needs: push-up progressions (incline, knee and full push-ups), table rows for your back, split squats for your legs, and isometric holds that start training your tendons.
Phase 2 (days 31-60) is bodyweight muscle building: feet-up push-ups, pike push-ups for your shoulders, pull-up negatives toward your first pull-up, chair dips and Bulgarian split squats, with progressive overload every week and protein for skinny guys who want to gain muscle.
Phase 3 (days 61-90) adds your first calisthenics skill: the tuck L-sit, the wall handstand or the planche lean (the first step toward the planche).
Take the test first: your most clean push-ups, your longest plank, your longest hang. Comment them like this: "Day 0: 12 / 45s / 20s", then come back on day 90 and reply with your new numbers.

entry.title: How Isometric Holds Give You Supernatural Strength (Full Guide)

media:group.media:title: How Isometric Holds Give You Supernatural Strength (Full Guide)
media:group.media:description:
Ever noticed how some skinny guys can push, pull or hold things a much bigger guy can't move? It's not muscle. It's isometrics, training by holding still. This is the full guide: by the end, you'll know everything you need to start isometric training at home, with no weights.
🧱 Free home plans and self-tests: https://www.reptheory.online/
🤝 Train with the free community on Telegram: https://t.me/thereptheory
What's inside: • Why holding still works: your muscles produce more force holding still than when they're lifting, and your brain learns to fire everything at once.
• Hold 1, the bottom of a push up: your strength test. The "push the floor away" cue, what 10, 20 and 30 seconds feel like, the sagging-hips mistake, and how to make it easier or harder.
• Hold 2, the deep split squat: why isometric strength is angle specific, why the bottom position carries over best to real movements, and the mistake of drifting up when you get tired.
• Hold 3, overcoming isometrics: pushing or pulling something that won't move (a towel curl, a palm press, a door frame), going from zero to everything in an instant, and how to breathe through it.
• Hold 4, the hollow body hold: the position gymnasts build almost everything on, the lower-back cue, and the beginner version.
• Hold 5, the wall handstand: how to walk up the wall, the "push the floor away" cue, the banana-back mistake, and the pike hold if you're not ready yet.
• Hold 6, the L sit: from the tuck L sit on two chairs to a full L sit, plus the feet-down version everyone starts with.
• The rule: the "two dials" (long holds at 7 out of 10, short all-out pushes) and three mistakes that waste your holds.
• Questions everyone asks: can holds replace weights? Will they make you bulky? Can you do them every day? How long should each hold be? Why do your muscles shake? Plus the blood pressure finding nobody expects.
• A full week you can copy: Monday, Wednesday and Friday sessions of about 15 minutes, a 5-minute version for busy days, and what to expect over 12 weeks.
• Your test result: what your push-up hold time means and which hold to start with.

Research mentioned: Oranchuk et al. 2019 (Scand J Med Sci Sports: review of 26 studies; holds at long muscle lengths built more muscle, explosive intent built faster force, tendons need 70%+ effort); Lum & Barbosa 2019 (Int J Sports Med: isometric strength is angle specific; how to hold for size and for maximum strength); Edwards et al. 2023 (Br J Sports Med: a review of 270 trials; isometric training lowered resting blood pressure the most of the exercise types tested); the force-velocity relationship (muscles produce more force holding still than while lifting); Moritani & deVries 1979 (early strength gains are mostly neural). The push-up hold levels are our own rough guide, not a medical or fitness assessment.

Make sure any chair, wall or bar you use is solid and the space around you is clear. Stop if you feel sharp joint pain. If you're under 18, skip the all-out pushes and keep everything at a medium effort.
